Standing on the Causeway

How might it matter that one was written before independence and the other on the day a state was proclaimed?
2. Choose one passage from Hind Swaraj. Quote it in a few words, then explain in your own words what Gandhi says that self-rule requires of Indians themselves, and not only of the British.
3. The Declaration of Israel gives reasons for the new state. Choose one of the reasons it gives. Quote it in a few words and explain it. Then use the lesson “Palestine, Israel, and the Arab World” to say how a Palestinian Arab reading the same document in 1948 might respond, and why.

4 pts		 Reads both sources accurately and draws on specific details from each, along with what the week's lessons taught. Reads both sources accurately but uses few specific details, or leans on only one. Shows partial understanding of one or both sources, with some errors or vague claims. Misreads the sources or does not refer to them.

4 pts		 Connects each claim to evidence and compares the sources with care. Explains why a speaker's purpose, position, and moment matter. Supports most claims with evidence. The comparison is sound but not fully developed. States conclusions with little support, or describes the sources without comparing them. Offers opinions without evidence from the sources.
Clarity and precision of expression
4 pts		 Writes in clear, well-organized sentences. Quotations are short, accurate, and introduced. Treats each people's account with fairness. Writing is clear with minor lapses in organization or precision. Writing is often unclear or disorganized, and quotations are unclear or misplaced. Writing is too unclear to follow.
Intellectual honesty
4 pts		 Names the limits of what each source can show and says what remains uncertain without overclaiming. Acknowledges at least one limit of the evidence. Mentions limits only in passing, or claims more than the sources allow. Treats each source as complete and beyond question.

16 pts total

assignments.title: 36.5 VR Activity: Follow the Container
assignments.html:
VR ACTIVITY
Follow the Container
Solo · one in-headset session
🎯 WHAT YOU'RE DOING

In 1956 a single ship carried fifty-eight truck bodies packed in its hold, and the shipping container changed how the world trades. In your VR headset you will follow a container through a reconstruction of a modern port and the chain that carries goods from a factory to a shop. Your task is to find evidence of who gains and who is strained along the way.

💻 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset, charged and ready
▶
Your course page for this week, which lists the session link and the place to enter
▶
A notebook or open document for quick notes while you are in the session
▶
About 45 minutes in one sitting
🔒 HOW TO JOIN
Where to go: Open your immersive session from the link on your course page, then enter the location named there.
Solo or group: Solo. You do not need a partner.
If something fails: Write down what happened and use the help contact on your course page. Do not skip the activity.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Review first. Reread the sections of the lesson “A Globalizing World: Trade, People, and Science” called Trade Without Walls and Uniting or Dividing. Remember that cheaper shipping let goods be made far from where they are sold, and that the gains and costs fell on different people.
2
Start at the factory end. Begin where the goods are made or loaded, and note how the work is organized and how many people it needs.
3
Follow the box. Move with a container from the ship to the crane, the train, and the truck. Notice how little a person has to open or touch it along the way.
4
Stop at three places. Choose three spots that show a gain or a cost of this system. At each one, capture a picture with your headset and jot a note about what you see.
5
Look for the people. At each spot, ask who has a job because of this system, who might have lost one, and who is not on the chain at all.
6
Write your response. After you leave the session, write one paragraph of about 150 to 200 words that answers this question: Who gains and who is strained along this chain, and what can a model of a port never tell you about the people whose lives depend on it?
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT

Submit your three captured images and your paragraph in the Canvas assignment. Use the images as evidence in your writing, and name which picture you are referring to.

Estimated time: 45 minutes

✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I followed a container from the ship to the end of the chain.
☐
I captured three images that show different parts of the port or chain.
☐
My paragraph uses at least two of my images as evidence.
☐
My paragraph connects what I saw to what I read about trade and globalization in the lesson “A Globalizing World: Trade, People, and Science”.
☐
I wrote in complete sentences and kept to about 150 to 200 words.
👨‍🏫 FACILITATOR NOTE

Teacher-facing. Before releasing this activity, add the session link and the specific location to the course page, and confirm that students have a way to capture images in their headsets. The instructions above assume a walkable reconstruction of a container port and its supply chain. If none is available, substitute another walkable space that shows how goods move around the world, such as a model of a factory and a shipping route, and adjust the steps and review section to match, and note the substitution in the teacher's manual. The instructions are platform-neutral on purpose. Grade with the course rubric for VR activities: three images as evidence, a paragraph that cites them, and reasoning tied to the lesson.

quizzes.title: 20.5 Reading Quiz: The Dutch Republic
quizzes.description: This quiz covers both lessons in this module: The Dutch Republic. It has 9 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: Philip II tried to rule his empire by reading and answering reports in Madrid. Why did this habit weaken his hold on the Low Countries?

answers.text: His governors in Brussels secretly sided with the rebels and ignored the reports he sent them.
He could not afford couriers, so reports reached him only once a year, if at all.
Answers to urgent questions took weeks to arrive, by which time events had often changed.
He refused to read reports written by Protestant subjects, so he never heard their grievances.

questions.text: The Duke of Alba's rule united groups that had little reason to cooperate before. Which of his actions did the most to bring Catholics and Protestants, nobles and merchants, together against Philip?

answers.text: He executed loyal Catholic nobles such as Egmont and Hoorn and imposed a heavy sales tax.
He allowed Calvinist crowds to destroy statues and stained glass in churches across the provinces.
He moved the seat of government from Brussels to Madrid, far from the people it ruled.
He arrested William of Orange and held him in Brussels as a warning to the other nobles.

questions.text: In 1574 the people of Leiden were starving, yet the city was saved by flooding the countryside. Why did the flood help the rebels and not the Spanish?

answers.text: The water destroyed the Spanish fleet before it could reach the coast, ending the siege at sea.
The flood washed away Leiden's walls so that the rebel army could march straight into the city.
The Spanish soldiers could not swim and drowned in large numbers as the water rose around them.
Rebel ships with shallow bottoms could sail over the drowned fields as the Spanish pulled back.

questions.text: William of Orange was killed by an assassin in 1584, but the revolt did not collapse. Which explanation best fits the lesson?

answers.text: Philip II ended the war at once, because he feared the growing power of the Dutch navy at sea.
His son Maurice rebuilt the army, and local councils kept governing in the name of the provinces.
The Catholic southern provinces took over the fighting and drove the Spanish out by 1585.
The English queen sent an army across the sea that finished the war within a few years.

questions.text: In 1576 Spanish soldiers sacked Antwerp and killed thousands of its people, though Philip had not ordered it. What does the lesson suggest was the underlying cause?

answers.text: Antwerp had refused to pay taxes to the Spanish crown for several years, and the soldiers came to collect.
William of Orange had hidden his army inside the city, and the Spanish moved in to drive it out.
Their pay was months and years behind after Philip's bankruptcy, so the soldiers mutinied.
Alba had ordered an example to be made of the Protestant cities that had joined the revolt.

questions.text: Hugo Grotius argued that the sea was open to the ships of every nation. Yet the Dutch East India Company often shut out rivals once its own ships controlled a trade. What does this suggest?

answers.text: The Dutch applied the principle when it helped them and dropped it once they held the trade.
The company had never heard of Grotius's argument and acted entirely on its own interests.
Grotius's pamphlet was really written to defend Portugal and its claim to the Asian trade.
The company had lost interest in trade and wanted only to rule islands as a government.

questions.text: The Dutch East India Company sent fleets on voyages that lasted years. Why did the chance to resell shares at the bourse help it raise money?

answers.text: The government promised to repay every investor's losses if a fleet failed to return home safely.
Investors could sell their shares instead of waiting years for a fleet to come home.
Only the richest merchants of Amsterdam were allowed to own shares, which kept the risk low.
Investors were paid in spices instead of coins, so the company never had to find any cash.

questions.text:
The Sea Beggars were privateers, sailors who attacked enemy ships with a prince's permission, and they had been using English ports as their base. In the spring of 1572 Queen Elizabeth closed those ports to them. Some six hundred men in a fleet of small ships were suddenly without a harbor, and they went looking for one on the Dutch coast. They found Brielle almost undefended and took it on the first of April.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: The Sea Beggars were privateers whose attacks on Spanish shipping caused nearly every rebel success.
answers.feedback: This is true of what the Sea Beggars were, but the passage is about how one town was taken, not about every rebel success.

answers.text: Queen Elizabeth secretly ordered the Sea Beggars to take Brielle so that Spain would lose a Dutch port.
answers.feedback: The passage says Elizabeth closed her ports to the Sea Beggars. It does not say she ordered the attack on Brielle.

answers.text: Brielle had been guarded so poorly that any rebel force could have taken it at any time that year.
answers.feedback: The passage says Brielle was almost undefended, but only in the spring of 1572 and only as the men searched for a harbor. It does not say any force could have taken it at any time.

answers.text: The Sea Beggars took Brielle largely by accident, after the loss of their English harbor sent them searching.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage traces the loss of the English harbor, the search for a new one, and the almost undefended town, so the capture followed from circumstance, not from a plan.

questions.text:
Foreign visitors remarked that Dutch merchants dressed plainly, kept honest weights, and paid their debts, and that a handshake in Amsterdam counted for a great deal. Look at what that good name could buy. The Dutch cities could borrow money at lower interest than the king of Spain, who had defaulted again and again.

Which choice most logically completes the text? Taken together, these sentences suggest that the Republic's reputation for honest dealing was ________

answers.text: a habit that mattered little, since the king of Spain could borrow as cheaply as any Dutch city.
answers.feedback: The passage says the cities borrowed at lower interest than the king, so he could not borrow as cheaply as they could.

answers.text: a kind of wealth, because lenders accepted lower interest from borrowers they trusted to repay.
answers.feedback: Correct. Trust that debts would be repaid is what let the cities borrow at lower cost.

answers.text: a benefit to Amsterdam's merchants alone, because lenders in other towns had never heard of it.
answers.feedback: The passage speaks of Dutch cities borrowing cheaply, not of Amsterdam's merchants alone, and says nothing about lenders in other towns being unaware of the reputation.

answers.text: a danger, because honest borrowers were pressed to take on more debt than they could repay.
answers.feedback: The passage gives no sign that honest borrowers were pushed into debt. It says the reputation lowered their cost of borrowing.

quizzes.title: 22.5 Reading Quiz: England: Crown and Parliament
quizzes.description: This quiz covers both lessons in this module: England: Crown and Parliament. It has 9 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: Charles I ruled for eleven years without calling Parliament, and he raised money through ship money. John Hampden refused to pay it, and the judges ruled for the king by only a narrow vote. What does the close vote suggest?

answers.text: Most English people supported the king's right to tax without asking Parliament for approval.
Many subjects doubted that the king could tax without consent, even though he won the case.
The judges were divided over whether Parliament still existed after eleven years of silence.
Ship money had always been charged to the whole kingdom, so very few people objected to it.

questions.text: In 1640 Charles called a Parliament after years of ruling without one. What forced him to do so?

answers.text: Seven bishops had petitioned him to call one, and a jury had cleared them of any wrong.
Parliament had offered him a large loan in return for ending the ship money tax.
Puritans in New England had sent a petition that he could no longer afford to ignore.
He had no money for an army against the Scots, and only Parliament could vote the taxes.

questions.text: In January 1642 Charles marched into the House of Commons with armed men to arrest five members. Why did this make war much more likely?

answers.text: No king had ever entered the Commons by force, and what trust remained between the two sides broke down.
It killed several of Parliament's leaders and left the Commons without a voice of its own.
It ended the Long Parliament and made Charles an absolute ruler of England from then on.
It caused the Scots to invade England again that spring, which began the fighting.

questions.text: At Putney in 1647, soldiers and officers argued over who should vote. What does this debate show about the effect of the civil war?

answers.text: The army agreed that the king should be restored to full power as soon as possible.
The Levellers and Henry Ireton agreed that every man in England should have the vote.
Once the old order cracked, people began asking who should rule and who should vote.
Parliament voted at once to give all men the vote after hearing both sides of the debate.

questions.text: The republic that followed the execution of Charles I did not last. Which explanation fits the lesson best?

answers.text: Charles II invaded England with a foreign army and defeated Cromwell's forces in a single battle.
It rested on Cromwell and the army, so it fell apart soon after he died in 1658.
The Scots took over the government in 1653 and handed the crown back to the old royal family.
Parliament voted to end the republic because it had become too expensive for England to keep.

questions.text: Many Protestants put up with James II for years. Which development in 1688 did the most to change their minds?

answers.text: The death of Charles II, which left the throne open to rival claimants from several families.
The passing of the Toleration Act, which gave Catholics the right to hold public office.
The conversion of his daughter Mary to Catholicism, which split the royal family in two.
The birth of a Catholic son, who now stood ahead of his two Protestant daughters.

questions.text: Parliament offered the crown to William and Mary only if they accepted the Bill of Rights. What does this show about the settlement of 1689?

answers.text: Parliament claimed power to limit the crown and even to decide who would wear it.
Parliament had abolished the monarchy and made William a servant of the Commons.
William had no legal claim to anything and was forced to leave England within a year.
James II kept the right to return to the throne if he accepted the Bill of Rights.

questions.text:
In 1647 army officers and common soldiers met in the church at Putney to debate what kind of government England should have. A group called the Levellers wanted most men to have the vote. Colonel Thomas Rainsborough said that "the poorest he that is in England hath a life to live, as the greatest he." Cromwell's son-in-law, Henry Ireton, answered that those with no property had no lasting stake in the kingdom. If they could vote, they might vote to take property away from others.

According to the text, why did Henry Ireton oppose giving the vote to men with no property?

answers.text: The poorest men were too uneducated to follow Parliament's debates or judge its leaders.
answers.feedback: The passage says nothing about education. Ireton's reason concerned property, not learning.

answers.text: The Levellers planned to use the new voters to bring Charles I back to power in England.
answers.feedback: The passage does not link the Levellers to the king's return. They wanted a wider vote.

answers.text: Men with no property had no lasting stake in the kingdom and might vote to take others' property.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage states Ireton's reason directly: no lasting stake, and the risk of votes taking property.

answers.text: A poor man's life counted for less than the life of a great landowner in the eyes of the law.
answers.feedback: This reverses Rainsborough's point. He said the poorest man had a life to live as the greatest did.

questions.text:
The Bill of Rights said what a king could not do, but a promise on paper was weak, as Charles I had shown with the Petition of Right. Parliament added a stronger tool. The Mutiny Act of 1689 allowed officers to punish soldiers for desertion and disobedience, and it expired after a year.

Which choice, if true, would most strongly support the claim that the Mutiny Act gave Parliament a firmer hold on the king than the Bill of Rights did?

answers.text: Charles I accepted the Petition of Right in 1628, and he went on ignoring its limits for years.
answers.feedback: This shows that a promise on paper can fail, but it says nothing about whether the Mutiny Act worked any better.

answers.text: Without a new act each year, the army could not be held together, so a king had to call Parliament yearly.
answers.feedback: Correct. It shows that the act made the king depend on Parliament every year, which a promise on paper could not do.

answers.text: William spent most summers across the Channel, commanding armies in the long war against Louis XIV.
answers.feedback: This is true, but it concerns William's wars and says nothing about Parliament's hold on the king.

answers.text: The Bill of Rights also said that elections had to be free and that members could speak freely in debate.
answers.feedback: This adds to what the Bill of Rights contained, but the claim is that the Mutiny Act was firmer than the Bill of Rights.

quizzes.title: 25.5 Reading Quiz: The Old Regime in Crisis
quizzes.description: This quiz covers both lessons in this module: The Old Regime in Crisis. It has 10 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: France had about three times as many people as Britain, yet Britain could borrow more money and at lower cost. What best explains this?

answers.text: British taxpayers paid higher rates than the French did, so lenders expected quick repayment from them.
The Royal Navy captured enough foreign treasure each year to cover the interest on every loan.
Lenders trusted Parliament, which set aside particular taxes, to repay what the nation borrowed.
The British king had promised to repay each loan from his own private estates and income.

questions.text: At Quebec in 1759 a single volley broke the French lines after Montcalm chose to attack at once. What does the lesson suggest about this victory?

answers.text: It owed much to a few quick choices and lucky chances, and it could have gone the other way.
It was certain from the start, because Britain had far more soldiers in Canada than France.
It ended the war at once, because Britain won in India and the Caribbean that same day.
It showed that the French army was weak everywhere and could not win a battle in Europe.

questions.text: In the Treaty of Paris, France gave up Canada but kept two small sugar islands. What does this choice suggest about how French ministers judged their colonies?

answers.text: They believed the sugar islands were easier to defend with the French navy than Canada was.
They wanted to punish the settlers of New France for refusing to pay taxes to the king.
They thought Canada was too close to the British colonies to be kept in peacetime.
They judged that the sugar islands were worth more to France than the snows of Canada.

questions.text: Why did Britain's victory in 1763 lead to a quarrel with its American colonies?

answers.text: The colonists wanted to join France after Britain took Canada from the French settlers.
The war debt had nearly doubled, so Parliament taxed colonists who had not given their consent.
Parliament had banned all trade between the colonies and the French sugar islands.
The king refused to send any soldiers to the frontier after the rising led by Pontiac.

questions.text: France helped the Americans win at Yorktown in 1781. What did this victory do for France?

answers.text: It gave France Canada back and returned its trading towns in India to French control.
It ended the French debt, because the Americans paid back the cost of the French fleet.
It brought revenge but no new land, and it added to a debt that France could not easily pay.
It made Louis XVI popular enough to reform the tax system without asking anyone to approve it.

questions.text: Calonne proposed a land tax on every owner of land. The Assembly of Notables refused it. What does their refusal suggest?

answers.text: The nobles and officials chosen to approve it were the people who would have lost their exemptions.
The Notables thought the king already had enough money from loans and did not need any new taxes.
The Notables feared that the tax would make bread too expensive for the poor of the cities.
The Notables had been told by the king to refuse so that he could blame them for the debt.

questions.text: A hailstorm in July 1788 flattened crops across northern France. How did the failed harvest change the situation when the Estates-General met?

answers.text: It destroyed the palace at Versailles, so the king had to hold the meeting in Paris instead.
It persuaded the nobles to give up their exemptions so that the poor could buy bread.
It made the king dismiss Necker, whose plan for the grain trade had failed that spring.
It filled the streets with hungry, angry people and left the king less room to delay.

questions.text: The Estates-General met in 1789 with a dispute over voting. Why did the method of voting matter so much?

answers.text: Voting by head would have let the Third Estate, with its doubled deputies, outvote the others.
Voting by estate would have given the Third Estate two votes, one more than the clergy.
Voting by head would have forced the king to attend every session of the Estates-General in person.
Voting by estate would have ended the privileges of the clergy and the nobles at once.

questions.text:
Borrowing felt painless at the time. Necker raised money by selling life annuities and lottery loans at high rates of interest, and none of it required a new tax. But every loan had to be repaid with interest, and interest was paid out of future taxes. A king who borrows to avoid a quarrel with the privileged has not avoided it. He has only put it off, and made it larger.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Necker showed that France could avoid taxing the privileged by finding lenders who accepted high interest.
answers.feedback: This reverses the passage, which says the quarrel was only put off. It was not avoided.

answers.text: Borrowing spared the king a quarrel with the privileged for a time, but it made that quarrel larger later.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage as a whole says borrowing delayed the quarrel and enlarged it.

answers.text: Necker's loans failed because lenders refused to buy life annuities or lottery loans from the crown.
answers.feedback: The passage says Necker did raise money this way. It does not say that lenders refused.

answers.text: The privileged classes agreed to pay new taxes in the 1780s so that the king could repay his loans.
answers.feedback: The passage says the loans required no new tax. It does not say the privileged agreed to pay one.

questions.text:
British ministers had an answer to the colonists' complaint. They said that every member of Parliament spoke for all British subjects, whether or not those subjects had voted for him, and that the colonists were represented just as the people of Manchester and Birmingham were, towns that sent no members at all. The colonists thought this a thin argument. A member who had never seen Boston, they said, could tax it without ever feeling the tax himself.

Which choice most logically completes the text? The colonists' objection to being taxed by this Parliament was that ________

answers.text: the people of Manchester and Birmingham had been taxed more heavily than the colonists had.
answers.feedback: The passage mentions Manchester and Birmingham only as the ministers' example of towns without members. It does not compare their taxes with the colonists'.

answers.text: members of Parliament were chosen by the king and not by any voters, in Britain or in the colonies.
answers.feedback: The passage does not say who chose the members. The colonists' point is about distance and about who feels the tax.

answers.text: the colonists had never been asked to pay a tax of any kind before the war with France began.
answers.feedback: This goes beyond the passage, which speaks only of the colonists' complaint about this Parliament's taxing them, not about every earlier tax.

answers.text: a body whose members did not share the burden could vote a tax on people it did not know.
answers.feedback: Correct. The colonists said a member who had never seen Boston could tax it without feeling the tax himself.

quizzes.title: 27.7 Quarterly Exam: Quarter 3: Early Modern Europe
quizzes.description: This exam covers this quarter only, weeks 19 to 27. It has 41 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

questions.text: Cortés founded the town of Veracruz and had its council elect him captain. Why was this a clever move?

answers.text: It gave him legal title to the Mexica capital before he had even seen the city.
It made him answer to the town and the king, not to the governor he had defied.
It freed him from paying the king's share of any gold that he might find.
It persuaded the people of the coast that Spain had already conquered them.

questions.text: Cortés marched inland and met towns such as Cempoala that hated paying tribute to Tenochtitlan. What did this show about the Mexica empire?

answers.text: Its conquered towns kept their own rulers and gods, so they felt like loyal members of one Mexica people.
Its subjects were held mainly by fear and tribute, so a challenger could turn them against it.
Its main weakness was a lack of soldiers, since it had never fought a war of conquest.
Its rulers had already agreed to share power with their old enemies in the city of Tlaxcala.

questions.text: Why did the capture of Atahualpa at Cajamarca do so much damage to the Inca state?

answers.text: News of the capture reached Cusco too slowly for any general to answer it.
The Inca armies had been destroyed at Cajamarca, so nothing was left to defend the empire.
Atahualpa ordered his generals to surrender as soon as he was seized.
All authority flowed from one man, so his generals hesitated to risk the emperor's life.

questions.text: The viceroy Toledo revived the old mita at Potosí. How did the Spaniards change its purpose?

answers.text: The Inca paid it in silver coins. The Spaniards collected it in grain.
The Inca required it only in wartime. The Spaniards made it a yearly festival.
The Inca used it for roads and farms. The Spaniards used it for the mines.
The Inca forced only the rich to serve. The Spaniards made the poor serve.

questions.text: In 1581 the northern provinces declared that Philip II had lost the right to rule them. What reason did they give?

answers.text: He had died without leaving an heir to the throne of the Low Countries.
He had refused to learn Dutch after more than twenty years on the throne.
They said that he had broken his duties as a king toward his subjects.
He had lost the war at sea and could no longer defend their ports.

questions.text: Spanish soldiers sacked Antwerp in 1576, and for a short time all seventeen provinces stood together. What happened to that unity?

answers.text: It faded, and by 1579 the mostly Catholic south made peace with Philip.
It lasted until 1648, when Spain finally accepted Dutch independence.
It ended when Philip paid his soldiers and the outrage was forgotten.
It broke when William of Orange was shot and the provinces blamed each other.

questions.text: Why did Amsterdam grow so fast after 1585?

answers.text: The new stock exchange offered free land to anyone who would build a house there.
The Spanish king moved his court to Amsterdam to be closer to the war.
The Dutch East India Company hired thousands of sailors from the Baltic.
Spain captured Antwerp and closed its river, so merchants and bankers fled north.

questions.text: The lesson calls Dutch toleration practical, and not equality. Which detail shows its limits?

answers.text: Jews were forbidden to build a synagogue in any Dutch city.
Only Calvinists held high office, and Catholics worshiped in secret.
Catholics held most high offices in the towns of the Republic.
Only people born in the Republic were allowed to trade in Amsterdam.

questions.text: The potato took a long time to win acceptance in Europe, yet it changed northern populations. Why?

answers.text: It grew well in cold, wet climates, and a small plot could feed a family.
It was cheaper to ship than wheat, so cities bought it in place of bread.
The Church urged the poor to eat it during the many fast days of the year.
It could be stored for years without spoiling, so no one starved in winter.

questions.text: Why did sugar lead to large plantations rather than small farms?

answers.text: The Crown forbade small farmers to grow sugar, so only nobles could plant it.
Cane grew only on islands where no other crop would grow.
Cane needed much land, costly mills, and a great deal of labor.
Planters wanted to keep the price of sugar high by limiting the supply.

questions.text: According to the lesson, how did African states take part in the Atlantic slave trade?

answers.text: They took no part, since the Europeans seized all captives far inland.
Powerful states such as Asante and Dahomey sold captives from their wars.
They banned the trade at once and fought the Europeans along the coast.
They bought captives from Europeans and put them to work on plantations.

questions.text: In 1781 the captain of the Zong had about 130 sick captives thrown into the sea. How did a court treat the case?

answers.text: As a murder trial, and the captain was hanged for the crime.
As a mutiny, and the sailors who refused the order were punished.
As a matter for the Admiralty, and it was never brought before a judge.
As a dispute about money, since the owners claimed insurance.

questions.text: In 1628 Parliament made Charles I accept the Petition of Right. What did he do next?

answers.text: He refused to sign it and sent Parliament home that same day.
He kept it faithfully for eleven years and called Parliament each spring.
He asked the judges to declare it void, and they agreed unanimously.
He agreed to it, and then he simply ignored it when it suited him.

questions.text: What was new about the New Model Army that Parliament created in 1645?

answers.text: It was paid by the king, who had agreed to share command with Parliament.
Officers rose by ability and not by birth, and soldiers were paid regularly.
It was made up of foreign soldiers hired from the Dutch Republic.
It was open only to Puritans who had sworn the Scottish Covenant.

questions.text: William of Orange had his own reasons to accept the invitation of 1688. What was one?

answers.text: He wanted to end the Dutch Republic by joining it to the English crown.
He had been promised a large sum of money from the English Parliament.
He wanted England as an ally against Louis XIV and not as France's friend.
He hoped to convert the English people to the Dutch Calvinist church.

questions.text: What did the Act of Settlement of 1701 show about the new English government?

answers.text: Parliament could choose the king, which no one imagined in 1600.
The king could now tax without consent so long as he called Parliament once a year.
The Church of England had taken over the power of choosing the king.
The crown would pass only to a Catholic cousin of the late king.

questions.text: Why did Louis XIV make the nobles compete for places in his daily ceremonies at Versailles?

answers.text: He wanted them to learn the arts so that France would have a better army.
Only the king could grant pensions, offices, and army commands to them.
He had no other way to collect the taxes that they owed to the crown.
He wished to keep them away from the army, which was run by his ministers.

questions.text: The lesson says Louis XIV's rule was less absolute than it looked. Why?

answers.text: Offices were bought and inherited, and old privileges of the towns limited him.
Parliament in Paris met every year and approved each tax that he asked for.
The nobles kept private armies, so he could not give orders to the provinces.
His ministers were chosen by the great families of France, and not by the king.

questions.text: Why was the revocation of the Edict of Nantes a gift to Louis XIV's rivals?

answers.text: The Huguenots took the French navy with them and sold the ships to the Dutch.
The Huguenots led a rebellion in southern France that forced Louis to leave Paris.
Protestant kings refused to trade with France after the edict was issued.
About two hundred thousand skilled Huguenots fled to his enemies abroad.

questions.text: The Nine Years' War is an early example of the balance of power. What does that mean?

answers.text: A strong ruler can keep peace in Europe by giving every state the same size of army.
Each state trades only with those countries that have an equal navy.
A state that grows strong enough to dominate its neighbors makes them unite against it.
Smaller states hand over their armies to the strongest state for protection.

questions.text: Why did Newton's success give educated people a new confidence?

answers.text: It proved that the Church had been wrong about the Bible for fifteen centuries.
It gave kings the power to tax all trade between Europe and Asia.
It showed that nature followed laws that mathematics could describe.
It showed that careful observation was useless without a university degree.

questions.text: Frederick the Great and Catherine the Great liked Enlightenment ideas. What does the lesson say about their reforms?

answers.text: They shared power with elected parliaments that wrote the new laws.
They ended monarchy in their lands and handed power to the philosophes.
They banned the Encyclopédie in their courts and burned the copies.
They reformed from above and did not give up their own power.

questions.text: A ruler seizes his subjects' property and jails them without cause. Whose argument says that the people may resist him?

answers.text: Locke's, since a ruler who attacks their rights loses his claim to obey.
Montesquieu's, since only independent judges may remove a king from office.
Voltaire's, since a king is bound to follow the advice of the philosophes.
Smith's, since no government may take part in the buying and selling of goods.

questions.text: What does Adam Smith's pin factory illustrate?

answers.text: The invisible hand: a king should set the price of every pin to be fair.
The division of labor: ten workers doing separate steps make thousands.
The social contract: workers agree to obey the owner who gives them wages.
The separation of powers: one worker cuts the wire and another sells the pins.

questions.text: How did Frederick the Great help Britain in the Seven Years' War?

answers.text: Paid with British money, he kept French armies busy in Europe.
He sent the Prussian navy to help the British fleet attack Quebec.
He agreed to take the Ohio Valley and give Canada to Britain.
He lent Pitt a large army that sailed to India under Clive.

questions.text: How did a trading company become a ruler in India?

answers.text: The Mughal emperor sold Bengal to the company to pay for his armies.
Clive won at Plassey, and the company took control of rich Bengal.
The French company left India and handed all its forts to the British.
Parliament sent a royal army that conquered Bengal in a single summer.

questions.text: Who bore the heaviest burden of taxation in the France of Louis XVI?

answers.text: The nobles, who paid the taille and the tithe on their own estates.
The clergy, who paid a tenth of their land to the crown each year.
The merchants, who paid the salt tax and no other tax.
Commoners and peasants, while nobles and clergy were mostly exempt.

questions.text: What did Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès argue in his pamphlet of 1789?

answers.text: That the king should give up his throne and a republic should be declared.
That the clergy and nobles should each have two votes in the Estates-General.
That the Third Estate was the whole nation and now deserved to be something.
That the Estates-General should meet every year in the city of Paris.

questions.text: What did the Assembly do on the night of August 4, 1789?

answers.text: It voted to remove the king from his throne and declared a republic.
It sold the lands of the Church and used the money to pay the army.
It gave the vote to every man and woman over the age of twenty-one.
It ended the tithe, many feudal dues, and the rights of nobles.

questions.text: The Declaration of the Rights of Man says that men are born free and equal. What tension does the lesson point out?

answers.text: It guarded the rights of the nobles but not those of the commoners.
It gave the king the power to veto any law that the Assembly passed.
It said "man" and meant men, and slavery continued in the colonies.
It required all citizens to belong to the Catholic Church.

questions.text: How did France raise so large an army by 1794?

answers.text: The king of Prussia lent soldiers to the Convention in return for land on the Rhine.
The levée en masse of 1793 called all French people to serve the war.
The Church paid for an army of volunteers to defend the faith.
The Vendée peasants joined the army in order to defend the Republic.

The settlement gave every national group its own state and ended all disputes over borders.
The new states had been chosen by plebiscite, so the people had accepted the new borders.

questions.text: In January 1918 elections gave the Bolsheviks only about a quarter of the seats in the new assembly, and Lenin dissolved it. What does this suggest about Lenin's view of the party?

answers.text: He believed that the assembly was too large to govern Russia well during the civil war.
He planned to hold a second election as soon as the Whites had been defeated in the war.
He believed a disciplined party should lead the nation, even against the wishes of the voters.
He wanted to give the soviets the right to run all later elections in place of the assembly.

questions.text: Weimar Germany seemed stable by 1925, but the Great Depression hit it especially hard. Why?

answers.text: The new government had refused all American loans and had no money to put people to work.
The republic's recovery stood on borrowed money, and American lenders called in their loans.
The Depression began in Germany, and from there it spread across the sea to the United States.
German factories had been destroyed in the war, so Germany had nothing to sell abroad.

questions.text: Stalin's Five-Year Plan built steel towns and heavy industry very fast. Who paid the main price?

answers.text: The factory workers, whose wages were cut to pay for the new machines and the steel towns.
The nobles, whose lands were taken and given to the soldiers who had fought for the Reds.
The Communist Party members, who were sent to the new steel towns against their will.
The peasants, whose farms were seized, and millions of whom starved in the famine.

questions.text: In the March on Rome in 1922 the army could have stopped the Fascists, but the king did not call it out. What does this suggest about how Mussolini came to power?

answers.text: The Fascists had a larger army than the Italian government, so resistance was hopeless.
Mussolini had already won a majority in parliament, so the king had no choice.
His rise was not unavoidable, because it turned on the king's choice not to use the army.
The king agreed with Mussolini's plan to invade Ethiopia and wanted him in power.

questions.text: Hitler became chancellor in January 1933. Which description fits the lesson?

answers.text: It was legal but not inevitable, because conservative leaders believed they could control him.
It was a violent coup, in which Nazi troops seized the capital and forced Hindenburg to resign.
It was certain from 1928, when the Nazis won a majority of the votes in a national election.
It was the result of a popular vote in which Hitler won more than half of all voters.

questions.text:
By late 1923 prices were doubling in days, and the German mark stood at several trillion to the American dollar. Workers were paid twice a day, and wives waited at the factory gate to rush the notes to the shops before they lost their value. Families whose savings, pensions, and insurance had been counted in marks found them worth less than a loaf of bread. Those who owed money could pay off a debt with a handful of notes.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Hyperinflation made German money almost worthless and wiped out the savings of ordinary families.
answers.feedback: Correct. The details of falling prices, rushed shopping, and ruined savings all show one thing: money lost its value.

answers.text: German workers earned far higher wages in 1923 because they were paid twice each day.
answers.feedback: Workers were paid twice a day because the notes lost value so fast, not because their wages had risen.

answers.text: The American dollar became the official money of Germany at the end of 1923.
answers.feedback: The passage compares the mark with the dollar to show how far the mark had fallen. It does not say that the dollar replaced it.

answers.text: Only families who owed money suffered in 1923, since debts could be paid with a handful of notes.
answers.feedback: This is too narrow, and it leaves out the families whose savings were ruined. The passage says debtors benefited, but it does not say they were the only ones affected.

questions.text:
Stalin's rise rested on timing and patience. Lenin, ill in his last months, dictated notes warning that Stalin was too rude and had gathered too much power, and he suggested removing him as General Secretary. The party leaders chose not to publish the notes.

Which choice, if true, would most strongly support the claim that a different choice by the party leaders could have changed the course of Stalin's career?

answers.text: Magnitogorsk was built beside an iron mountain by workers living in tents and barracks.
answers.feedback: This is a fact about one industrial project. It says nothing about how Stalin gained or could have lost power.

answers.text: Trotsky was later exiled and, in 1940, murdered in Mexico on Stalin's order.
answers.feedback: This shows what Stalin did to a rival after he had power. It does not show that removing him earlier could have changed his career.

answers.text: Stalin used his post as General Secretary to build a following within the party.
answers.feedback: Correct. If his post as General Secretary was what let him build a following, then removing him from it, as Lenin suggested, could have changed his career.

answers.text: The Five-Year Plan set targets from above and raised them when factories fell short.
answers.feedback: This describes how the plan worked, not how Stalin rose, so it does not bear on the claim.

quizzes.title: 34.5 Reading Quiz: The Cold War and Communism
quizzes.description: This quiz covers both lessons in this module: The Cold War and Communism. It has 10 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: At Yalta, Stalin agreed to free elections in Eastern Europe, but by 1946 Soviet-backed communists were taking power there. What best explains his actions?

answers.text: He believed that the Western powers had already broken the agreement by dividing Germany.
He had never seen the text of the agreement and learned of it only after the Red Army left.
He wanted a ring of friendly states around Russia and trusted only governments he controlled.
He wanted the satellite states to accept American money to rebuild their cities after the war.

questions.text: Why did Secretary of State Marshall propose to help rebuild Western Europe?

answers.text: Hunger and poverty fed the appeal of communist parties, and recovery would weaken it.
Britain had asked America to take over its colonies and needed money to defend them.
The satellite states had asked for American loans, and Stalin had agreed to allow them.
The United Nations had ordered the richest nations to pay for Europe's rebuilding.

questions.text: When Stalin blockaded West Berlin, Truman refused to give way but did not want a ground war. What does the Berlin Airlift show?

answers.text: The Western powers had given up on West Berlin and were helping its people to leave.
The blockade had already failed, because Soviet troops let the trucks through at night.
The Americans and British had planned to attack East Germany by air if the blockade continued.
It resisted the blockade without risking a war on the ground between the two sides.

questions.text: The lesson tells of a Soviet submarine near Cuba in 1962 where one officer refused to agree to launch a nuclear torpedo. What does the story suggest?

answers.text: The Soviet navy had ordered its submarines to attack American ships on sight near Cuba.
The danger was greater than leaders knew, and much rested on individual judgment.
The American ships had agreed to leave the area as soon as they spotted the submarine.
The crisis was never close to war, since the officers on the submarine had no real power.

questions.text: Factories in the Soviet Union met their quotas by making goods nobody needed, and shops had long lines and empty shelves. What does this suggest about a command economy?

answers.text: Planners had no prices to signal what was scarce, and workers had little reward for good work.
Soviet workers were lazier than workers in other countries and did not wish to produce more.
The government had ordered the factories to make too few goods so that prices would stay high.
The planners had made too many mistakes in arithmetic when they set the production targets.

questions.text: The Great Leap Forward led to the worst famine in history. Which cause does the lesson give?

answers.text: Mao ordered the army to take the harvest from the peasants to feed the cities.
The Soviet Union cut off all grain to China after the two countries quarreled.
Harvests were neglected, and officials reported false numbers to please their superiors.
A severe drought lasted three years, and the government refused all foreign help.

questions.text: Gorbachev told the leaders of the satellite states that the Soviet Union would no longer send in tanks. The lesson calls this the decisive choice. Why?

answers.text: It allowed the Soviet Union to move its troops home and spend the money on the economy.
Once the fear of Soviet tanks was gone and people could speak freely, the system began to unravel.
It made the leaders of the satellite states resign at once, so that elections could be held.
It meant that Gorbachev had given up on reform and was planning to retire from the party.

questions.text: On November 9, 1989, East German guards gave way when crowds rushed to the Berlin Wall. What does the lesson suggest about why the Wall opened?

answers.text: The guards had received an order from Moscow to open the gates in the Wall that night.
The government had planned for years to open the Wall and had told the guards to wait.
The crowd was armed, and it forced the guards to leave their posts at the crossing points.
A confused announcement left the guards without orders, in a state with no will to use force.

questions.text:
By 1961 about three million East Germans, many of them young and skilled, had left for the West, most of them through Berlin. In August the East German government built a wall of concrete and barbed wire across the city. Its guards were told to shoot those who tried to cross. President John Kennedy protested but did not send troops, judging that war was too high a price.

According to the text, why did President Kennedy protest the building of the Wall but not send troops?

answers.text: He agreed with the East German government that the Wall would stop the flow of people to the West.
answers.feedback: The passage says Kennedy protested. It does not say he agreed with the Wall.

answers.text: He judged that war was too high a price, so he protested but sent no troops.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage states his reason directly: war was too high a price.

answers.text: He feared that American soldiers would be shot by East German guards who had been told to fire.
answers.feedback: The passage says guards were told to shoot those who tried to cross the Wall, not American soldiers.

answers.text: He had no power to act, because Congress had ordered him not to use troops in Europe.
answers.feedback: The passage gives the reason as Kennedy's own judgment. It says nothing about an order from Congress.

questions.text:
In 1968 the Czechoslovak leader Alexander Dubcek tried to build "socialism with a human face" in the Prague Spring, with more freedom of speech. Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev sent in troops from the Warsaw Pact. The Brezhnev Doctrine declared that the Soviets would act whenever socialism was threatened in a member state.

Which choice most logically completes the text? After 1968, a communist leader in the bloc who wanted to reform his country could expect that ________

answers.text: Soviet troops might be sent in, since the Soviets claimed the right to act whenever socialism was threatened.
answers.feedback: Correct. The doctrine declared that the Soviets would act whenever socialism was threatened, so reform carried that risk.

answers.text: the Warsaw Pact would defend his reforms, since its members had promised to protect each other's freedom.
answers.feedback: The passage shows the Warsaw Pact troops entering Czechoslovakia, not defending its reforms.

answers.text: the Soviets would leave him alone as long as he kept freedom of speech out of the newspapers and schools.
answers.feedback: The passage says nothing about a bargain over newspapers. It names the Soviet right to act as the rule.

answers.text: Western countries would send troops to protect him, as they had in Hungary twelve years earlier.
answers.feedback: The passage does not mention the West or any earlier events in Hungary, and it shows no troops coming to Dubcek's defense.

quizzes.title: 36.7 Quarterly Exam: Quarter 4: Late Modernity
quizzes.description: This exam covers this quarter only. It has 41 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

questions.text: Why did industrialization begin in Britain and not somewhere else?

answers.text: Britain had more people than any other country, so it had more workers for its mills.
The Crown ordered the building of the first factories and paid for each of them.
Cheap coal and fairly high wages made machines that saved labor a good bargain.
Britain had banned the export of cotton, so its mills had no foreign rivals.

questions.text: How did Watt's improved steam engine change where factories could be built?

answers.text: It could turn a wheel, so a factory no longer had to sit beside a fast river.
It could run on wood alone, so factories could be built far from the coal mines.
It was small enough to be built into each worker's cottage.
It made the water wheel faster, so more factories were built on rivers.

questions.text: What did the Factory Act of 1833 do that earlier appeals had not?

answers.text: It banned all work by women and children in every kind of factory.
It set a ten-hour day for every worker in every trade.
It gave the workers the right to vote in the next election.
It created paid inspectors to see that the law was kept.

questions.text: Marx expected the workers of the most industrial country to rebel first. What happened in Britain?

answers.text: The workers rose in 1848 and the army put down the revolt in a few days.
Wages rose, unions grew, and Parliament widened the vote for workers.
The mill owners gave their factories to the workers and left the country.
Parliament banned all unions and the workers were too afraid to protest.

questions.text: What did the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819 do?

answers.text: They gave each German state a written constitution and an elected assembly.
They put universities under watch, banned student clubs, and censored books.
They joined Austria and Prussia into a single country under one emperor.
They freed the peasants of Prussia from the dues that they owed to the nobles.

questions.text: Why did the Frankfurt assembly of 1848 fail to unite Germany?

answers.text: The Austrian army occupied Frankfurt on the first day of the meeting.
The assembly voted to unite with France and the Germans refused to follow.
The assembly could not agree on a language for the new constitution.
The Prussian king refused its crown, and the assembly had no army to back it.

questions.text: How did Garibaldi help to unite Italy?

answers.text: He took the south with a force of volunteers and handed it to the king.
He defeated the Austrians at Solferino and took Venetia for Piedmont.
He persuaded the pope to give up Rome and join the new kingdom.
He led the army of Piedmont in the war of 1859 and signed the peace.

questions.text: How did Bismarck use the telegram from Ems in 1870?

answers.text: He kept it secret so that France would be taken by surprise.
He sent it to the Austrians to persuade them to join Prussia.
He edited it to sound sharper, and the French government declared war.
He published it unchanged to prove that the French had insulted the king.

questions.text: Which developments helped Europeans conquer so much of Africa after 1870?

answers.text: Railways that crossed the whole of Africa before 1850 and cheap iron ships.
Alliances with every African ruler and the consent of the Berlin conference.
Large European armies that landed in Africa and stayed for several years.
Steamships, the telegraph, quinine, and the Maxim gun gave Europeans an edge.

questions.text: Why did Ethiopia keep its independence when most of Africa did not?

answers.text: Britain and France agreed at Berlin that Ethiopia should be left alone.
Menelik II bought modern rifles, trained his army, and won at Adwa.
Ethiopia had no valuable land, and the Europeans were not interested.
The emperor signed a treaty that made Ethiopia a protectorate of Italy.

questions.text: What event in 1839 turned the dispute over the opium trade into the First Opium War?

answers.text: The Qianlong Emperor refused Macartney's request for freer trade in 1793.
The Taiping rebels attacked the British ships at Shanghai.
Lin Zexu destroyed British opium, and merchants demanded payment.
Britain wanted to stop the sale of opium in China, and China refused.

questions.text: What did the samurai of Satsuma and Choshu learn from the Western bombardments of 1863 and 1864?

answers.text: Swords could not expel foreigners; they had to learn Western ways.
The shogun was strong enough to defeat the Western ships without their help.
Japan should sign treaties with every nation and give up its own army.
The emperor should give up his throne and move to the city of Edo.

questions.text: How did the Schlieffen Plan make war more likely in 1914?

answers.text: It called for a quick blow at France before the slower Russians could mobilize.
It required Germany to wait for an attack by France before it could mobilize.
It promised Britain that Germany would respect the neutrality of Belgium.
It asked Austria to attack Russia first and then take the Balkans.

questions.text: Why does the lesson call the death of Franz Ferdinand ironic?

answers.text: He was killed by an assassin sent by his own government.
He had ordered the driver to turn right on that street.
He had often argued against going to war with Serbia, fearing for his empire.
He had planned to give Bosnia to Serbia within a year.

questions.text: Why did attacks on the Western Front so often fail?

answers.text: Both armies lacked shells, and they could not keep up their bombardments.
Machine guns and artillery gave the men defending a trench line a decisive advantage.
The armies were too small to man a line that ran from the Channel to Switzerland.
The generals ordered every attack to begin in daylight, and soldiers refused.

questions.text: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare in January 1917. What did this help to bring about?

answers.text: The end of the British blockade of Germany and the return of food.
The surrender of Russia and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk.
The collapse of Austria-Hungary and the end of the Habsburg throne.
The entry of the United States into the war on the Allied side.

questions.text: Why did Clemenceau want a harsh peace?

answers.text: He believed Germany had been punished enough and wanted to move on quickly.
He wanted Germany to join the League of Nations as soon as possible.
France had lost over a million men and was invaded twice in fifty years.
He had promised Wilson that France would take no land from Germany.

questions.text: How did the Bolsheviks win the civil war against the Whites?

answers.text: Britain, France, Japan, and the United States sent large armies to help the Reds.
The Reds had many more soldiers than the Whites in every battle.
The Whites were driven out when Lenin gave land to the nobles.
The Whites were divided, and the Reds held the cities and railways.

questions.text: What caused the German hyperinflation of 1923?

answers.text: France occupied the Ruhr, and the government printed money to pay striking workers.
The Dawes Plan ended all American loans to Germany in 1923.
The stock market in New York crashed and the banks in Germany failed.
The Kaiser returned and ordered the treasury to pay his old soldiers.

questions.text: What did Stalin, Mussolini, and Hitler have in common, despite their differences?

answers.text: Each came to power by winning more than half of the votes in free elections.
One party, one leader, a secret police, and an enemy within.
Each was supported by the Church and by the old nobility.
Each ruled through an elected parliament that had real power over taxes.

questions.text: What did the Munich agreement of 1938 cost Czechoslovakia?

answers.text: Its alliance with France, which was ended at once by the French parliament.
Its mountain defenses, and in 1939 the rest of the country.
Its army, which was disbanded by order of the four powers.
Its government, which was moved to London during the war.

questions.text: How were the Germans able to defeat France in about six weeks in 1940?

answers.text: Tanks crossed the Ardennes, a forest that the French thought impassable for armor.
They broke through the Maginot Line with heavy artillery in a single week.

Moctezuma never met Cortés before the Spaniards entered the city.

The Crown gave all of the silver to the Church, which spent it on buildings.

He fought the Turks and the Dutch rebels, and the bills were too large.

answers.text: The French army's strength in open battle did little good against a hostile population in Spain.

answers.text: Napoleon lost soldiers in Spain mainly because couriers and foragers deserted.
answers.feedback: This changes a detail. The passage says foragers disappeared but never says anyone deserted.

questions.text:
Newton's ideas had to win over doubters, and they did it by measurement. Newton's theory said that the Earth bulges at the equator and is flatter at the poles. Many French scientists, who had followed Descartes, expected the opposite. In the 1730s the Academy of Sciences sent expeditions to Peru and to Lapland, in the far north of Europe, to measure the length of a degree of the Earth's curve.

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: The results agreed with Newton's prediction, and doubters began to give way.
answers.feedback: The first sentence says Newton's ideas won by measurement, so the results must have favored him.

answers.text: The results were unclear, and French scientists kept to Descartes's view for another century.
answers.feedback: This contradicts the first sentence, which says measurement won over the doubters.

answers.text: The results agreed with the French scientists' expectation, and Newton's theory was set aside.
answers.feedback: This reverses the outcome. The passage says Newton's ideas won, not those of the French scientists.

answers.text: The Academy cancelled the expeditions after deciding that the question could not be settled by measurement.
answers.feedback: The passage says the expeditions were sent and that measurement did the persuading, so they were not cancelled.

questions.text:
The result was that British silver flowed to China to pay for tea. The British traders looked for something the Chinese would buy, and they found it in opium, grown in British India and smuggled into China. The East India Company grew the opium in Bengal and sold it at auction in Calcutta to private traders, who carried it to the China coast and sold it to Chinese smugglers. That way the Company could say it never sold opium in China.

According to the text, how could the East India Company say it never sold opium in China?

answers.text: It sold the opium to Chinese officials at Canton, who passed it on to the emperor.
answers.feedback: The passage says the buyers were private traders and Chinese smugglers, not officials.

answers.text: It grew the opium in China, where the emperor allowed it to be sold freely.
answers.feedback: The passage says the opium was grown in Bengal and smuggled into China, not sold with the emperor's leave.

answers.text: It sold the opium only to the British government, which shipped it to China.
answers.feedback: The passage names private traders as the buyers, not the British government.

answers.text: It sold the opium at auction in Calcutta to private traders, who carried it to China.
answers.feedback: The Company's sale ended in Calcutta, and private traders took the opium from there.

questions.text:
The Shah ruled as a modernizer. In the 1960s his "White Revolution" gave land to peasants, gave women the vote, and built schools and factories. But he ruled as an autocrat, banned real opposition, and relied on a secret police called SAVAK. Oil money flowed in, and the gap between the wealthy and the poor grew.

Which choice would best support the conclusion that many Iranians turned against the Shah?

answers.text: Iran's oil was developed by a British company.
answers.feedback: This is true, but it says nothing about how Iranians felt toward the Shah.

answers.text: In January 1978 students and clerics protested in Qom, and police killed some of them.
answers.feedback: Public protests against the government, met by killings, show opposition. This is direct evidence.

answers.text: Britain answered Mossadegh's oil law with a boycott that choked Iran's income.
answers.feedback: This is true, but it concerns Mossadegh and Britain, not Iranians' view of the Shah.

answers.text: The White Revolution gave women the vote and built schools and factories.
answers.feedback: These reforms are in the passage as the Shah's modernizing side, and they do not show opposition.

questions.text:
Metternich saw this clearly, and he set out to hold the line. In 1819 a student named Karl Sand murdered the conservative writer August von Kotzebue. Metternich used the event to push the Carlsbad Decrees through the German Confederation. They put universities under watch, banned student societies, and censored the press. Spies and police were common. Revolts that broke out in Spain and Naples in 1820 were put down by foreign troops. Austrian soldiers marched into Naples, and in 1823 a French army crossed the Pyrenees into Spain. Britain refused to take part.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Metternich won the support of all the great powers, Britain included, for crushing revolts.
answers.feedback: The last sentence says Britain refused to take part, so not every great power joined him.

answers.text: Metternich met demands for national states with censorship at home and foreign armies abroad.
answers.feedback: It joins the two parts of the passage: control at home through the Decrees, and foreign troops against revolts abroad.

answers.text: Metternich thought that student societies and a free press would strengthen the German Confederation.
answers.feedback: This reverses the passage, which says he banned student societies and censored the press.

answers.text: Metternich gave way to the revolts of 1820 after a student murdered a writer.
answers.feedback: The murder gave Metternich a reason to act, and the revolts were put down by foreign troops, so he did not give way.
