quizzes.title: A.8 Reading Quiz: Voyages and the Historian's Tools
quizzes.description: This quiz covers “The Age of Exploration: Voyages and Sponsors” and “Keeping Time, Asking Questions, Remembering Who We Are”. It has 7 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: The Portuguese caravel could sail against the wind better than older ships. Why did this matter so much on the African coast?

answers.text: Pirates hid in the bays along the coast and chased slow ships back out to sea.
Harbors there were too shallow for any ship with large square sails to enter safely.
Winds there blow south, so a ship that sailed south easily still needed a way to get home.
African rulers would trade only with captains whose ships could leave in a single day.

questions.text: Portugal's royal advisors told the king not to pay for Columbus's plan. What did they believe?

answers.text: Asia lay much farther west than Columbus claimed, so the voyage would run out of food.
The Atlantic was already claimed by Spain, and a Portuguese ship would be seized.
Columbus was too old to command a fleet and would be unable to hire a crew.
A sea route to Asia already existed around Africa, so a western route was needless.

questions.text: Dias reached the southern tip of Africa in 1488 and da Gama reached India ten years later. What did Dias's voyage make possible?

answers.text: It proved that the Spice Islands lay close enough to Lisbon to reach without stopping.
It gave Portugal a legal claim to all of Asia under the Treaty of Tordesillas.
It showed that the Indian Ocean lay open beyond the Cape, so a sea road to Asia could exist.
It showed that the Pacific could be crossed from the African coast in a single season.

questions.text: In 1609 the Dutch East India Company hired Henry Hudson to look for a northern route to Asia. What change in sponsorship does this show?

answers.text: Companies that raised money from many investors now paid for voyages alongside kings.
Kings were no longer interested in the spice trade and left exploration to private groups.
The Dutch crown gave up its claim to the sea in return for a share of all profits.
Captains now had to be citizens of the nation that sponsored the voyage they led.

questions.text: Ramadan falls in summer in some years and in winter in others. What explains this?

answers.text: The Islamic calendar counts years from a different starting date than the Christian one.
A lunar year is about eleven days shorter than a solar year, so lunar months drift through the seasons.
Muslims move the month by decision of the community each year to suit the harvest.
The month of fasting was set by early rulers to match the changing length of daylight.

questions.text: England did not adopt the Gregorian calendar until 1752, nearly two centuries after Catholic countries did. Which explanation fits the lesson best?

answers.text: The reform came from a pope, and Protestant England was unwilling to follow him.
English astronomers had proved that the older calendar was in fact more accurate.
English farmers needed the extra ten days to finish the harvest before the winter.
The English king feared that dropping days would make people late in paying taxes.

questions.text: Archaeologists found Richard III's skeleton under a parking lot in 2012. Why did identifying him take both documents and science?

answers.text: Radiocarbon dating alone gave his exact name, and the documents only agreed with it.
The skeleton had been moved many times, so no one could tie it to a place.
Documents pointed to the friary site, and dating and DNA confirmed the man.
Old chronicles were all lost, so only DNA could say where he had been buried.

quizzes.title: A.9 Reading Quiz: Reform and Atrocity
quizzes.description: This quiz covers “Democratic Reform Movements in Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, and Latin America” and “Genocide and Ethnic Cleansing: Cambodia, the Balkans, Rwanda, and Darfur”. It has 7 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: In 1975 Prime Minister Indira Gandhi jailed opponents and censored the press. In 1977 she called an election, lost, and left office. What does this show about India's democracy?

answers.text: Democracy survived partly because a powerful leader chose to obey the voters.
Her party was too weak to hold power, so the army removed her without a vote.
Elections in India were always so one-sided that no leader needed to worry.
The courts forced her out, and she had no say in the matter at all.

questions.text: Ghana began as a parliamentary democracy under Nkrumah but within a few years was a one-party state. How did this make the later coup easier to carry out?

answers.text: He gave the army so much power by law that it could dismiss any elected official.
He sold the nation's gold abroad, and soldiers were no longer being paid by anyone.
He had silenced the opposition, so there was no lawful way to remove him.
He banned the army and left the country with no force able to defend the government.

questions.text: In 1988 Chileans voted on whether Pinochet should rule for eight more years. Which combination best explains why the vote led to real change?

answers.text: The opposition united and watched the count, and Pinochet accepted the result.
A foreign army stood at the border and forced the general to accept the count.
The vote was secret, so Pinochet never learned how most people had voted.
The junta had already planned to step down and used the vote to announce it.

questions.text: Tiananmen in 1989, Myanmar in 1990, and Egypt in 2013 ended badly for reformers. What did these cases share?

answers.text: Each country's people had little interest in a change of government at all.
One institution, the army or a single party, held more power than any rival could check.
Each country had too many political parties for any one to govern the nation.
Each country was invaded by a neighbor soon after the reformers took power.

questions.text: A war that kills a great many people is not necessarily a genocide. What does the definition of genocide turn on?

answers.text: Whether the killing was done by a government instead of by a rebel army.
Whether more than one million people died, counting both soldiers and civilians.
Whether the aim was to destroy a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group as such.
Whether foreign nations had signed a treaty to stay out of the fighting.

questions.text: Most of the Khmer Rouge's victims were fellow Khmer, yet a court in 2018 convicted two leaders of genocide against the Vietnamese and the Cham. Why does this still leave lawyers debating the label for the whole slaughter?

answers.text: The court could not find that any killing had taken place in Cambodia.
Most victims were not from a group the Khmer Rouge targeted as a national or ethnic group.
The convicted men had served in the army and were not responsible for any killing.
Vietnam had already tried the leaders and the court was unable to try them again.

questions.text: Belgium gave every Rwandan an identity card stating his group. How did this later help the killers of 1994?

answers.text: It gave them the legal right under Belgian law to take the land of the Tutsi.
It taught young Rwandans to read, and so made radio broadcasts easier to spread.
It ended the old kingdom and with it every law that had once protected the Tutsi.
It fixed a loose difference into an official label that told them whom to target.

quizzes.title: A.10 Reading Quiz: Radicals and Religion in Russia
quizzes.description: This quiz covers “Russian Radicals and the War on Religion”. It has 6 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: Radicals killed Tsar Alexander II in 1881, and his son answered with harsher rule. Why was this an irony?

answers.text: The tsar's son had secretly supported the radicals and then betrayed them.
The radicals were all executed, so none of them lived to see the result.
The murdered tsar was the reformer, and the response ended moderate reforms.
The assassins were pardoned, and the tsar's own guards were punished instead.

questions.text: In 1874 thousands of students went to the villages to teach the peasants and stir them to revolt. Many were turned over to the police. What does this suggest about the peasants?

answers.text: They were pious and loyal to the tsar and distrusted the students' message.
They had already begun a revolt and did not need the help of the students.
They could not hear the students, who spoke only in a foreign language.
They wanted the landlords punished but feared the students would do the same.

questions.text: Lenin said that workers by themselves would only ask for better wages. What did he conclude they needed?

answers.text: A free press that could tell the whole country what the tsar was doing.
Leaders who would be chosen by all party members in a public vote.
A small, strict party of full-time revolutionaries to lead them.
A parliament in which every class could argue its case in the open.

questions.text: The Bolsheviks did not cause the February revolution of 1917, yet they took power in October. What gave them the advantage?

answers.text: Discipline and experience in underground work while the new government was weak.
Their huge membership, which easily outnumbered every other party in the country.
The support of the army, which had been won over by a long civil war.
A secret treaty with Germany that gave them money and soldiers to use.

questions.text: Why did the Soviet government treat the Russian Orthodox Church as a danger?

answers.text: It was the largest group outside party control, with a loyalty beyond the state.
Its priests had led an army that tried to put the tsar back on the throne.
Its clergy refused to pay taxes and spent all their wealth on missions abroad.
Its churches stood on land that the state wanted for new factories and roads.

questions.text: In 1943 Stalin allowed the Church to choose a patriarch. What does the timing suggest?

answers.text: The Church had won a long legal battle against the party in the courts.
He needed every ally in the war with Germany and eased the pressure for that reason.
He had given up his belief in atheism after reading the Bible during the war.
The Church had agreed to give all of its remaining land and property to the state.

quizzes.title: A.11 Reading Quiz: Regions and Migration
quizzes.description: This quiz covers “Regions, Rich and Poor: Reading the Map of the World” and “People on the Move: Why Migrants Leave and What Changes”. It has 7 questions with one correct answer each. Reread the lessons if you need to.

questions.text: The Sahel has thin, uncertain rainfall. Which pair shows a physical trait leading to a human trait there?

answers.text: Dense forest leading to fishing villages and large sea-going trading ships.
Tall mountains leading to terraced rice fields and a wet monsoon each year.
A cold climate leading to a dependence on timber and on iron smelted from bog ore.
Dry grassland leading to herding, millet farming, and caravan trade across the desert.

questions.text: Argentina was among the richest countries in 1900 and fell well behind, while South Korea went from poverty to wealth in two generations. What does this suggest?

answers.text: Choices by governments and citizens matter as much as geography does.
Countries with a long coast can never remain poor for more than a few decades.
Wealth depends only on the amount of oil or gold found beneath the ground.
Poor countries become rich only after they have been ruled by a foreign power.

questions.text: Why does Egypt fear the Ethiopian dam on the Blue Nile more than Ethiopia fears any Egyptian response?

answers.text: Ethiopia's land lies at sea level and cannot be damaged by changes in the water flow.
Egypt is nearly all desert and relies on the river for almost all its fresh water.
Egypt has no army, and Ethiopia has promised to attack any country that objects.
Egypt has no way to build dams of its own and must buy all of its electricity.

questions.text: The Aral Sea shrank after the 1960s. Who bore most of the harm?

answers.text: Sailors on the open ocean, who lost the shipping lanes of the Persian Gulf.
People living near the old shore, though a distant government made the choice.
The Soviet planners, who lost their cotton fields in a sudden flood.
Farmers in the mountains, who saw their rivers fill with salt from the sea.

questions.text: Which pair names a push factor and a pull factor in the Irish migration after 1845?

answers.text: The failure of the potato crop pushed people out, and better wages in America pulled them across.
Heavy taxes on grain pushed people out, and the cheap land in Canada pulled them across.
British soldiers pushed people out, and the free passage on Royal Navy ships pulled them across.
A lack of schools pushed people out, and the chance of a university degree pulled them across.

questions.text: West Germany expected its Turkish guest workers to stay a year or two, yet millions of their descendants are German citizens today. Which explanation fits best?

answers.text: The workers had been promised German citizenship before they arrived.
Turkey stopped accepting them back when the economy there slowed down.
Many stayed after recruiting ended in 1973 and brought their families.
Germany forced them to stay by closing its borders in 1961.

questions.text: Ciudad Juarez grew into a city of more than a million after 1965. What best explains the growth?

answers.text: A program let foreign factories build near the border, so workers moved north for jobs.
Mexico's government moved its capital there to be nearer its northern neighbor.
A great famine in the south forced the people of every village to migrate north.
A ban on trade across the river made Juarez a safe haven for refugees from Texas.

quizzes.title: A.12 Module Test: Supplementary Lessons
quizzes.description: This test covers all seven lessons in this module. It has 14 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

questions.text: The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 drew a line down the Atlantic. What was its purpose?

answers.text: To set the limits of the fishing waters that Portugal shared with England.
To keep Spain and Portugal from fighting over the lands they were finding.
To end the war between Spain and Portugal over the kingdom of Granada.
To divide the Pacific between the two nations after Magellan's voyage.

questions.text: Only one of Magellan's five ships returned to Spain, yet the voyage still mattered. What did it show?

answers.text: That cloves could not be grown in the Americas and had to be imported.
That the earth could be circled by sea and that the Pacific was vastly large.
That Portugal's route around Africa was too dangerous for regular use.
That the Atlantic was too wide for any further trade between Spain and Asia.

questions.text: Plutarch wrote his Parallel Lives to show Greek and Roman statesmen at their best and worst. What did he think history was?

answers.text: A record of treaties and laws whose dates a student ought to memorize.
A school of character, in which a reader learns how to act by watching others.
A set of cycles in which every empire must rise and fall in the same way.
A form of poetry meant to praise the rulers who paid for the books.

questions.text: The French revolutionaries' ten-day week was abolished by Napoleon in 1806. What does its failure suggest about calendars?

answers.text: A calendar must be based on the moon, or else it cannot serve a modern nation.
Governments can change a calendar only after a successful war abroad.
A calendar tied to worship and habit is hard for a government to change by order.
A calendar that begins from a new year number will always be thrown out.

questions.text: In 1986 Marcos claimed victory in the Philippines despite evidence of fraud. Why did he fall?

answers.text: The courts of his own country ruled that he could not stay in office.
His own party held a secret vote and replaced him with another leader.
Soldiers refused to fire on the peaceful crowds that filled the main avenue.
Foreign troops entered Manila and took control of the main government buildings.

questions.text: Nelson Mandela served only one term as president of South Africa. What example did this set?

answers.text: It showed that a president could rule only if every party had an equal vote.
It showed that a leader can give up power peacefully and build trust.
It showed that foreign governments chose the leaders of the new nation.
It showed that the army held the true power and the president was a figurehead.

questions.text: Srebrenica was declared a safe area by the United Nations, yet more than eight thousand men and boys were killed there. What made this possible?

answers.text: The town was far outside the area patrolled by any peacekeeper from any nation.
The United Nations had withdrawn its force a month earlier and left the town empty.
Dutch peacekeepers there had few soldiers and orders not to fight.
The Bosnian army had been ordered to hand over the town to the Bosnian Serbs.

questions.text: General Roméo Dallaire asked for more troops as the killing in Rwanda began. How did the Security Council respond?

answers.text: It sent a larger force within a week that stopped the killing in the capital.
It ordered the rebel army to withdraw from the capital until a vote was held.
It ended all talk of the war and left the matter to Belgium alone to settle.
It cut the size of the force that was already there.

questions.text: The Decembrists failed in a single day in 1825. Why do they matter to the story of Russian radicals?

answers.text: Their example and their wives' loyalty became a legend for later radicals.
Their plan became the model for the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917.
They won a constitution that every later tsar was required to respect.
They founded the first political party in Russia to hold regular elections.

questions.text: In 1967 Albania did something no other state had done. What was it?

answers.text: It allowed each region to choose its own religion and to tax its followers.
It gave its churches and mosques to the state and let believers use them in secret.
It declared itself an officially atheist state after closing most places of worship.
It signed a treaty with the Soviet Union that put its clergy under Moscow's control.

questions.text: Why does the Strait of Hormuz matter to countries thousands of miles from the Persian Gulf?

answers.text: Much of the world's seaborne oil must pass through one narrow channel.
The strait is the only place where ships can cross from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
The countries on the Gulf control most of the world's supply of fresh water.
The strait is the only route by which wheat can reach the cities of East Asia.

questions.text: Countries without a seacoast, such as Mali and Chad, tend to be poorer. Which reason does the lesson give?

answers.text: They have no deserts, and so their land is too wet to farm in most years.
Trade costs more because their goods must cross other countries to reach a port.
Their people are not allowed to leave and so cannot learn from other nations.
They have no rivers, and so they cannot grow food for their people.

questions.text: The 1947 partition of India divided Punjab. What was one effect?

answers.text: Every village in the region became home to a mix of Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs.
Cities only about thirty miles apart ended up on opposite sides of a hostile border.
The two halves of Punjab joined into a single province under Pakistani rule.
The region's farmers all moved east to the cities of Bengal and Assam.

questions.text: In 2015 many Syrian refugees traveled on to Europe. What was the effect on border areas such as the Greek islands and the Balkan roads?

answers.text: They became crowded, and governments quarreled over who should carry the load.
They were closed to all trade by order of the United Nations Security Council.
They emptied out, since no one wished to live near so many travelers.
They grew rich from the tolls that the migrants paid at each crossing.

quizzes.title: Quarter 3 Exam (SAT)
quizzes.description: This exam covers this quarter only, weeks 19 to 27. It has 36 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. Every question gives you a short passage taken from your lessons, so you can answer from the passage itself. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

questions.text:
Tlaxcala was a league of towns ringed on every side by Mexica territory. By most accounts its people had to do without goods such as salt and fine cotton cloth, because the trade routes ran through enemy hands. When the Spaniards arrived in September 1519, the Tlaxcalan leaders had to decide whether these strangers were a danger or a tool. They tested them in about two weeks of hard fighting. The horses and steel held, but both sides were worn down. The Tlaxcalan leaders then judged that men who could survive that fight would be useful against Tenochtitlan, and the offer cost them little at the start.

According to the text, why did the Tlaxcalan leaders offer the Spaniards an alliance?

answers.text: The two weeks of fighting had shown them that the Spaniards' horses and steel could not be resisted.
answers.feedback: The text says the horses and steel held but that both sides were worn down. It does not say the Spaniards could not be beaten.

answers.text: The Spaniards had promised to bring them salt and fine cotton cloth that the Mexica kept from them.
answers.feedback: The text says Tlaxcala lacked these goods because the trade routes ran through enemy hands. It mentions no promise from the Spaniards.

answers.text: They judged that men who survived two weeks of hard fighting would be useful against Tenochtitlan.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

answers.text: The Mexica had conquered them long ago, and they hoped the Spaniards would end the tribute they owed.
answers.feedback: The text describes Tlaxcala as ringed by Mexica territory, not as conquered or paying tribute.

questions.text:
Those politics were the key. As Cortés marched inland, he met towns that hated paying tribute to Tenochtitlan. The people of Cempoala joined him. The Tlaxcalans, who had never been conquered by the Mexica, fought the Spaniards hard and lost. Then they changed course and offered an alliance against their old enemy. Cortés saw that he did not have to beat the Mexica alone. He only had to find out who else wanted them beaten.

Which choice best supports the conclusion that the Spaniards did not defeat the Mexica on their own?

answers.text: Warriors from Tlaxcala and Texcoco did most of the fighting and destroying in the siege of Tenochtitlan.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

answers.text: Cortés had thirteen small warships built in pieces and carried to the lake to help seal off the city.
answers.feedback: This describes the Spaniards' own effort. It does not show that others did the fighting.

answers.text: Cortés wrote long letters to King Charles V to justify defying a governor and starting a war without permission.
answers.feedback: This concerns how Cortés defended himself to his king, not who won the war.

answers.text: Cortés ran his ships aground on the coast so that none of his men could turn back, and then marched inland.
answers.feedback: This shows Cortés's own commitment. It says nothing about help from others.

questions.text:
Here is how the mercury process worked. Water-driven mills crushed the ore to a fine powder. The powder was mixed with water, salt, and mercury and trampled by workers or animals for days. The silver clung to the mercury and formed a paste. When the paste was heated, the mercury boiled away and left the silver behind. The method had been developed in Mexico, and it let miners use ore that was too poor to smelt. It also needed a steady supply of mercury, which came mostly from a mine at Huancavelica in Peru, where the same kind of forced draft sent men underground. Some highland villages emptied as families moved away to escape the draft. The mine that fed Spain was fed in turn by the labor of people who had never agreed to it.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Silver ore was crushed, mixed with mercury, trampled into a paste, and heated until only silver remained.
answers.feedback: This describes the steps of the process, which is only one part of the passage.

answers.text: The Spanish conquest of the Americas rested on the forced labor of people who had never agreed to it.
answers.feedback: This is too broad. The passage is about the mining of silver, not the whole conquest.

answers.text: The mercury process was invented at Huancavelica and later taught to miners in Mexico.
answers.feedback: This distorts the passage, which says the method was developed in Mexico and that the mercury came from Huancavelica.

answers.text: Silver at Potosí was made by a mercury process that itself depended on forced labor from nearby villages.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

questions.text:
Pizarro's victory looks like Cortés's, but there are important differences. Pizarro had no large native army at his side at first. What he had was a plan that took advantage of how the Inca state worked. All authority in the empire flowed from one man. ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: A united native army would therefore have been easy for Pizarro to assemble.
answers.feedback: Nothing in the passage connects the flow of authority to raising a native army. The passage says Pizarro had none at first.

answers.text: Seizing that one man would therefore leave the entire system without a head.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

According to the text, what duty did the decree of 1793 give to women?

answers.text: To forge weapons and carry supplies.
answers.feedback: The text gives this duty to married men.

answers.text: To gather in the squares to rouse courage.
answers.feedback: The text gives this duty to old men.

answers.text: To fight with the army.
answers.feedback: The text gives this duty to young men.

answers.text: To make tents and nurse in hospitals.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

questions.text:
Robespierre was not a cruel man by temper, and that is what makes his case so troubling. He believed he was defending a pure cause against corrupt enemies. Once a leader decides that disagreement is treason, every critic becomes a traitor, and there is no limit to the list. A free republic needs ways to settle quarrels peacefully, and the Terror had destroyed them.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Robespierre was not cruel by temper, and that is what makes his case so troubling to historians.
answers.feedback: This is one point in the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Leaders who believe they serve a pure cause always destroy the republics that they claim to defend.
answers.feedback: This is too broad. The passage discusses one leader.

answers.text: Robespierre's belief in a pure cause led him to treat any disagreement as treason against it.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

answers.text: Robespierre knew his critics were innocent but had them killed anyway to protect his own power.
answers.feedback: This distorts the passage, which says he believed he was defending a pure cause against corrupt enemies.

questions.text:
His most lasting work was the Napoleonic Code of 1804, a single set of laws for the nation. In the old France the law had differed from province to province, and a family dispute could turn on where you happened to live. A commission of lawyers drew on Roman law and the older customs, and Napoleon sat in on many of its sessions himself. The Code kept the great gains of 1789: equality before the law, an end to feudal privilege, protection of property, and religious freedom. But it also ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: ended equality before the law for most men.
answers.feedback: The passage says the Code kept equality before the law.

answers.text: restored the feudal privileges of the old nobility.
answers.feedback: The passage says the Code kept the end of feudal privilege.

answers.text: gave husbands wide power over wives and children.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

answers.text: let each province keep its own laws.
answers.feedback: The passage says the Code was a single set of laws for the whole nation.

questions.text:
His men followed him because he won, and because he promised that a soldier could rise as far as his talent would carry him. Many of his marshals had been sergeants or sons of innkeepers. That promise tied the army to him more than it tied it to any government.

Which choice best supports the idea that the army was loyal to Napoleon more than to the government?

answers.text: In 1797 Napoleon negotiated the Campo Formio peace himself while the Directory looked on.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

answers.text: Napoleon was especially good at mathematics, a skill that suited the artillery branch.
answers.feedback: This describes his schooling, not the loyalty of the army.

answers.text: Murat rode across Paris in the night to bring up cannon before the crowd could seize them.
answers.feedback: This describes one night's defense, not the army's loyalty.

answers.text: Napoleon married Josephine de Beauharnais, a widow, two days before leaving for the front.
answers.feedback: This is a fact about his marriage, not the army's loyalty.

questions.text:
But in October 1813, at Leipzig, the "Battle of the Nations," Russia, Prussia, Austria, and Sweden defeated Napoleon. That autumn the allies offered peace that would have left him on the throne of a France that kept the Rhine and the Alps as its frontiers. Napoleon was slow to answer, and by the time he agreed, they had hardened their terms. ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: His slowness persuaded the allies to soften their terms again before the end of the year.
answers.feedback: The passage says the allies hardened their terms because he was slow.

answers.text: His slowness cost him a peace that would have let him keep the throne of France.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

answers.text: His quick agreement allowed him to keep the Rhine and the Alps as his frontiers.
answers.feedback: The passage says he was slow, not quick.

answers.text: His slowness gave him time to rebuild the army that had won the great battle at Leipzig.
answers.feedback: The passage says he lost at Leipzig.

questions.text:
Napoleon carried equality before the law, the end of feudal privilege, and his Code across Europe. In Germany and Italy, people who welcomed those reforms came to resent the foreign army that had brought them. He also silenced the press, ended elections, and fought wars that cost millions of lives. His rise was possible only because of the Revolution, but his rule undid its promise of liberty. Both parts of the story are true. Next week you will see how the winners at Vienna tried to rebuild Europe, and why they could not make the world go back.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Napoleon carried equality before the law, the end of feudal privilege, and his Code across Europe.
answers.feedback: This is only half of the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Revolutions always end by destroying the liberty they promised to protect, as this one did.
answers.feedback: This is too broad. The passage discusses one revolution.

answers.text: People in Germany and Italy rejected Napoleon's reforms because they disliked the ideas themselves.
answers.feedback: This distorts the passage, which says they welcomed the reforms and resented the foreign army.

answers.text: Napoleon spread the Revolution's reforms across Europe but also ended its liberty at home.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

questions.text:
Read the passage below. Then answer the ten questions that follow it.

1  Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva, the son of a watchmaker, and his mother died days after his birth. He ran away from his apprenticeship at sixteen. He was an outsider among the philosophes. In 1750 he won a prize from the academy of Dijon with an essay arguing that the arts and sciences had corrupted morals. Voltaire read his next essay, on inequality, and joked in a letter that it made him want to walk on all fours. Where they praised progress, he worried that civilization had made people vain and unequal. In The Social Contract, published in 1762, he opened with a famous line: "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains."

2  For Rousseau, a government is legitimate only when it follows the general will, the common good of the whole people, expressed when citizens make their own laws. He separated it from the will of all, which is only the sum of what each person wants for himself. A citizen who refused to obey the general will, he wrote, could be compelled to, and he called this being forced to be free. He admired the citizen virtue of early Rome and of Sparta. Critics ask a hard question: who decides what the general will is? Revolutionaries would later claim to speak for it. Rousseau did not choose how others would use his words. In 1762 French authorities condemned his Social Contract, and he had to flee France. Geneva, the city he was proud to call home, burned it too. He also believed that citizens would only love their country if they shared festivals, schools, and a common education that taught them to put the public good first.

3  Rousseau had little patience with the English government that Montesquieu admired. In The Social Contract he wrote that the English people thought themselves free but were free only on election day. Once they had chosen their representatives, he said, they were slaves again. A people who let others make their laws had given up the very thing that made them free. He thought that real self-government was possible only in small states, such as the Swiss cantons and the old city-republics he admired.

4  Adam Smith was a Scottish professor of moral philosophy and a friend of the philosopher David Hume. In the 1760s he traveled in France as a tutor and met Voltaire and the French economists. In 1759 he argued that people feel sympathy for one another and judge their own conduct by imagining how a fair observer would see it. In 1776 he published The Wealth of Nations. In it he described the division of labor. In a pin factory, he said, ten workers who each do one step can make thousands of pins a day. Smith counted about eighteen separate steps in a pin: one worker draws the wire, another straightens it, a third cuts it, a fourth sharpens the point. Ten workers who each made whole pins might make only a few hundred. By Smith's count, the ten men together could make more than forty thousand pins in a day.

5  Smith had left his professor's chair at Glasgow in 1764 to tutor a young duke on a tour of France, and the lifetime pension he earned for the work gave him time to write. The Wealth of Nations took about ten years. It was published in March 1776, and the first edition sold out in about six months. Smith later took a post as a customs commissioner in Edinburgh, which let him see for himself the trade rules he had criticized.

6  He wrote that a nation's wealth lay in what its people could make and buy, not in a pile of gold and silver. He thought that, under just laws, people who pursue their own interest can serve the public good as if guided by an invisible hand. He used that phrase only once in The Wealth of Nations. In the same book he wrote, "It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest." He also criticized slavery as unjust and wasteful. But he took justice, law, and good character for granted. A market without them would not work. Smith was also no flatterer of businessmen. He warned that when merchants of the same trade meet, the conversation usually ends in a plot against the public or a scheme to raise prices.
According to the passage, what did Rousseau say about the English people?

answers.text: They were free only because they lived in a small state like the Swiss cantons, which he admired.
answers.feedback: Rousseau thought real self-government was possible only in small states, but he did not say the English lived in one.

answers.text: They were free only on election day, then slaves again once they had chosen representatives.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate the part of the passage the question names, then match it to what the passage states.

answers.text: They had given up their freedom by letting the English king make all of their laws for them.
answers.feedback: The passage says he criticized letting representatives make the laws, not the king.

answers.text: They were more free than any other people because their elected Parliament made their laws.
answers.feedback: This reverses his point. He thought a people who let others make their laws had given up what made them free.

questions.text: As it is used in paragraph 6, the word regard most nearly means

answers.text: admiration and respect for.
answers.feedback: This is a common meaning of the word, but the sentence says the butcher acts from self-interest, not admiration.

answers.text: a long, careful look at.
answers.feedback: This fits the word's literal sense of looking, which does not work with someone's own interest.

answers.text: agreement and approval of.
answers.feedback: Self-interest does not mean agreeing with one's own interest, and the sentence does not use the word that way.

answers.text: careful consideration of.
answers.feedback: Correct. Put each choice into the sentence in place of the word and keep the one that preserves the sentence's meaning.

questions.text: Which choice best describes Rousseau's attitude toward the English system of representation, as paragraph 3 presents it?

answers.text: Skeptical, because he doubted that electing representatives made a people free.
answers.feedback: Correct. Find the words that carry judgment, then match both the direction and the strength of the attitude.

answers.text: Admiring, because he praised it as the best and freest government of his time.
answers.feedback: The passage says he had little patience with it, while Montesquieu was the one who admired it.

answers.text: Furious, because he thought the English people deserved to be punished for their folly.
answers.feedback: This is too strong. He criticized the system, and the passage shows no hatred of the people.

answers.text: Indifferent, because he gave the English system very little thought at all.
answers.feedback: He commented on it directly and sharply, so he was not indifferent.

questions.text: In paragraph 2, the sentences "Critics ask a hard question: who decides what the general will is? Revolutionaries would later claim to speak for it." mainly serve to

answers.text: show that Rousseau fully supported the later Revolutionaries.
answers.feedback: The passage says Rousseau did not choose how others would use his words.

answers.text: prove that the critics had completely misunderstood the general will.
answers.feedback: The sentences present the critics' question as a hard one, not as a mistake.

answers.text: raise a doubt about how Rousseau's idea could be used.
answers.feedback: Correct. Ask what job the sentences do for the paragraph, not just what they are about.

answers.text: explain why Rousseau had to flee France after 1762.
answers.feedback: The passage gives the reason in a later sentence, the condemnation of his book.

questions.text: The passage most strongly suggests that Smith believed the "invisible hand" works when

answers.text: people pursue their own interest, whatever laws or habits exist.
answers.feedback: The passage says he took justice, law, and good character for granted and that a market without them would not work.

answers.text: people pursue their own interest under just laws and good character.
answers.feedback: Correct. Find what the passage establishes, then choose the answer that needs the fewest added assumptions.

answers.text: merchants of the same trade meet together and agree on prices.
answers.feedback: The passage says Smith warned that such meetings usually end in a plot against the public.

answers.text: the phrase is repeated again and again throughout The Wealth of Nations.
answers.feedback: The passage says he used the phrase only once.

questions.text: Which choice best describes the organization of the passage?

answers.text: An account of Rousseau's ideas and critics, then an account of Smith's life and ideas.
answers.feedback: Correct. Say in a few words what each part does, then match the movement of the passage to the choice.

answers.text: A debate in which Rousseau and Smith answer each other's arguments point by point in turn.
answers.feedback: The passage never has either writer answer the other.

answers.text: A history of the whole Enlightenment arranged by date, from the 1750 essay to the 1776 book.
answers.feedback: The dates appear, but the passage is organized around two writers, not a timeline.

answers.text: An argument that Smith's ideas were better and more practical than Rousseau's.
answers.feedback: The passage describes both and does not rank them.

questions.text: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

answers.text: Smith's example of the pin factory shows how dividing the work among many workers raises output.
answers.feedback: This is one example from the passage, so it is too narrow to be the main idea.

answers.text: Enlightenment thinkers all agreed that people are born free and that markets should be left alone.
answers.feedback: This is too broad, and it distorts the passage, where Rousseau and Smith disagree and neither wants everything left alone.

answers.text: Rousseau and Smith offered different ideas about freedom and wealth, each with limits or risks.
answers.feedback: Correct. Read the whole passage, separate the central point from the examples, and reject choices that are too narrow, too broad, or distorted.

answers.text: Rousseau and Smith argued that governments should leave citizens and merchants entirely alone.
answers.feedback: This distorts both writers. Rousseau wanted citizens to be compelled to follow the general will, and Smith assumed just laws.

questions.text: According to the passage, which sequence of events led to the writing of The Wealth of Nations?

answers.text: The book earned Smith a pension, and he then left his professorship to tutor a young duke on a tour of France.
answers.feedback: This reverses the order. The pension came from the tutoring, and the book came after.

answers.text: Smith became a customs commissioner in Edinburgh, and that post gave him time to write the book.
answers.feedback: The passage says the customs post came later and let him see the trade rules he had criticized.

answers.text: Smith met Voltaire in France, and Voltaire paid him a pension so that he could write the book.
answers.feedback: The passage says the pension came from his work as a tutor, not from Voltaire.

answers.text: Smith left his professorship to tutor a duke, and the pension he earned gave him time to write.
answers.feedback: Correct. Name the relationship, find both ends in the passage, and check which event comes first.

questions.text: Based on the passage, how would Rousseau most likely judge a large nation whose citizens vote only to choose lawmakers and never on the laws themselves?

answers.text: He would doubt that its citizens were truly free, since self-government suits only small states.
answers.feedback: Correct. Find the principle the passage shows, restate it, and test each choice against the passage's own logic.

answers.text: He would praise it, since electing representatives lets even a large state remain free and self-governing.
answers.feedback: This reverses his view that a people who let others make their laws have given up what makes them free.

answers.text: He would approve it, so long as its laws add up to the sum of what each citizen wants for himself.
answers.feedback: This confuses the general will with the will of all, which the passage says is only the sum of private wants.

answers.text: He would call it as free as England, which he held up as the model of a free people to follow.
answers.feedback: The passage says he had little patience with England's system and called its people free only on election day.

questions.text: According to the passage, by Smith's count, how many pins could ten workers who each did one step make in a day?

answers.text: Only a few hundred pins.
answers.feedback: This is what the passage says ten workers who each made whole pins might make.

answers.text: More than forty thousand pins.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate the part of the passage the question names, then match it to what the passage states.

answers.text: Eighteen pins, one for each step.
answers.feedback: Eighteen is the number of separate steps Smith counted, not the number of pins.

answers.text: About a hundred thousand pins.
answers.feedback: The passage says more than forty thousand, not a hundred thousand.

questions.text: In a few sentences, describe the test-taking strategy you used on this exam. What did you do first, and how did you decide between answer choices?

Final question: record your answer.

Record a single video of about five minutes that answers all three questions below, one after another, in your own words. Speak in your own voice and do not read from a script. You may glance at brief notes, but each answer must explain the connections yourself, using at least two examples from the passages in this exam. You can record on a phone, a tablet, or a computer. Then upload that one video file here. Do not upload more than one file.

  1. In this quarter, Spain, France, and Britain all fought long, expensive wars. Using at least two of these countries, explain why the way a government raised and repaid its money mattered as much as how much money it had.
  2. Again and again in this quarter, a ruler lost control when the people he governed found someone offering them a different arrangement. Choose two cases from the exam and explain what they have in common and one important way in which they differ.
  3. Rousseau, Montesquieu, and Smith each offered a way to keep power from being abused. Choose one of them and use an event from the French Revolution or Napoleon’s rise, as it appears in this exam, to say whether that writer’s idea would have prevented what happened, and why.

quizzes.title: Quarter 4 Exam (SAT)
quizzes.description: This exam covers this quarter only. It has 36 multiple-choice questions with one correct answer each. Every question gives you a short passage taken from your lessons, so you can answer from the passage itself. You may reread your lessons before you begin.

questions.text:
Coal mines had a constant problem: water seeped in and flooded the shafts. In 1712 Thomas Newcomen built an engine that used steam to pump water out. It swallowed huge amounts of coal, but that hardly mattered at a coal mine, where fuel was nearly free. Anywhere else, coal had to be hauled in by cart, and the engine cost too much to run. So it stayed at the mines, and for half a century nobody did much better.

According to the text, why did Newcomen's engine stay at the mines?

answers.text: It was too heavy to move by cart, and no engineer had yet learned to make it smaller.
answers.feedback: The text gives the cost of running it, not its weight, as the reason.

answers.text: Parliament had given the mine owners a patent that kept the engine out of other businesses.
answers.feedback: The text mentions no such patent. It says the engine was too costly to run away from the mines.

answers.text: Coal was nearly free at the mines, while anywhere else the engine cost too much to run.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

answers.text: It could pump water only from deep shafts, so it was of no use in a factory or a mill.
answers.feedback: The text says the reason was the cost of coal, not what the engine could do.

questions.text:
Think about what that combination meant for a business owner. When workers are costly and fuel is cheap, a machine that saves labor and burns coal is a good bargain.

Which choice best supports the idea that machines that saved labor paid off in Britain?

answers.text: Hargreaves's spinning jenny let one worker spin many threads at once instead of one.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

answers.text: Newcomen, an ironmonger, built an engine that used steam to pump water out of coal mines.
answers.feedback: This describes who built the pump, not how labor-saving machines paid off.

answers.text: The Darby family were Quakers, Dissenters who were shut out of the universities and public office.
answers.feedback: This is a fact about religion and has nothing to do with labor-saving machines.

answers.text: After 1688 Parliament and the courts protected property, so an investor could keep what he earned.
answers.feedback: This explains why investors felt safe, not why machines that saved labor paid off.

questions.text:
Smith was no flatterer of employers when it came to wages, either. He wrote that masters were always and everywhere in a sort of quiet but steady agreement not to raise wages above their usual rate, and that when workers combined, the law came down on them far harder than it did on masters who did the same. A reader in the 1820s could set that remark beside the Combination Acts and draw a conclusion Smith himself might have shared.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: A reader in the 1820s could set Smith's remark beside the Combination Acts and draw a conclusion.
answers.feedback: This is only one sentence in the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Economists in Smith's day all agreed that employers should have no say in setting wages for their workers.
answers.feedback: This is too broad, and the passage does not say what other economists thought.

answers.text: Smith argued that workers should be forbidden to combine, since masters never did the same thing.
answers.feedback: This distorts the passage, which says the law was harder on workers than on masters who combined.

answers.text: Smith saw that employers quietly agreed to hold wages down, and the law fell harder on workers who combined.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

questions.text:
The same Parliament that passed the Factory Act reformed poor relief in 1834. Under the new Poor Law, an able-bodied man who asked for help had to enter a workhouse, where families were separated and the food was meant to be plainer than what a laborer could earn outside. The aim was to push men toward work and to cut the cost of relief. Many of the poor came to ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: prefer the workhouse to work in the mills and mines.
answers.feedback: The passage says the workhouse was made harsh on purpose, so few would prefer it.

answers.text: dread the workhouse and avoid asking for any kind of help.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

answers.text: welcome the new law as a generous reform of relief.
answers.feedback: The passage says the law was meant to push men toward work and cut the cost of relief.

answers.text: ignore the new law, since few were ever sent to workhouses.
answers.feedback: The passage says an able-bodied man who asked for help had to enter one.

questions.text:
The Congress nearly broke up over two prizes. Alexander wanted Poland, and Prussia wanted the German kingdom of Saxony, whose king had stayed loyal to Napoleon too long. Britain and Austria feared a Russia and a Prussia grown so large. Talleyrand saw his opening. He argued that the settlement should rest on legitimacy, and that the king of Saxony, whatever his faults, had a right to his throne. In January 1815 France joined Britain and Austria in a secret treaty to stand against Russia and Prussia if it came to that. War was close. The quarrel ended in a compromise. Russia received most of Poland, and Prussia received only part of Saxony, along with its lands on the Rhine.

According to the text, how was the quarrel over Poland and Saxony settled?

answers.text: Prussia received all of Saxony, and Russia received only part of Poland.
answers.feedback: This reverses the outcome the text gives.

answers.text: Russia received most of Poland, and Prussia received only part of Saxony.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

answers.text: Poland became an independent kingdom, and Saxony stayed whole under its own king.
answers.feedback: The text says Russia received most of Poland and Prussia received part of Saxony.

answers.text: Britain and Austria gave up both lands to avoid a war with Russia and Prussia.
answers.feedback: The text says Britain and Austria feared a larger Russia and Prussia and stood against them.

questions.text:
The diplomats showed prudence, which is the habit of weighing consequences before acting, and moderation toward the defeated. A harsher peace might have made France a permanent enemy.

Which choice best supports the claim that the diplomats were moderate toward France?

answers.text: In 1814 the diplomats joined Belgium to the Netherlands to guard against a French attack.
answers.feedback: This shows how the powers protected themselves from France, not moderation toward it.

answers.text: Talleyrand argued that the settlement should rest on legitimacy, since the king of Saxony had a right to his throne.
answers.feedback: This describes a point about Saxony, not how the powers treated France.

answers.text: Prince Metternich hosted the Congress, while its real work went on in small committees and private talks.
answers.feedback: This describes how the Congress worked, not how it treated France.

answers.text: In 1818 the powers withdrew their armies of occupation from France and admitted it to their councils.
answers.feedback: Correct. Identify the claim, then pick the direct evidence for it. The others are related to the topic but do not support this claim.

questions.text:
Was it the leaders, or was it deeper forces? In both countries, the answer is a mixture. Nationalism, railways, and trade made unity attractive and likely. But the actual shape of the new states depended on particular decisions: Napoleon III's secret bargain, Garibaldi's gamble, King William's choice of Bismarck, and Bismarck's restraint after Königgrätz. A Germany that included Austria was entirely possible. So was an Italy of two or three kingdoms. If Frederick William IV had accepted the crown at Frankfurt in 1849, a very different Germany might have been born.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

answers.text: Unity came from deep forces such as nationalism and railways, shaped by the choices of a few men.
answers.feedback: Correct. This is the organizing point of the whole passage, not just one detail or an overreach.

answers.text: Frederick William IV's refusal of the crown at Frankfurt in 1849 changed the shape of Germany.
answers.feedback: This is one example in the passage, so it is too narrow.

answers.text: Great nations are always made by strong leaders and never by the slow pressure of deeper forces.
answers.feedback: This is too broad, and it contradicts the passage, which gives both causes a place.

answers.text: Nationalism alone made unity certain, so the decisions of individual leaders made little difference.
answers.feedback: This distorts the passage, which says the shape of the new states depended on particular decisions.

questions.text:
Here Bismarck showed his judgment. The king and the generals wanted to march on Vienna and take land. Bismarck argued against it, so fiercely that he was close to resigning, until the Crown Prince helped to bring the old king around. He took no Austrian territory, because he wanted ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

answers.text: to leave land free for a later war against Austria.
answers.feedback: This reverses his reasoning. He argued against taking land so that Austria would not become an enemy.

answers.text: to please the generals who wanted a quick peace.
answers.feedback: The passage says the king and the generals wanted to take land, and Bismarck argued against them.

answers.text: Austria as a friend in the years that were to follow.
answers.feedback: Correct. The passage sets this up, and this choice follows from it with the fewest added assumptions.

answers.text: to avoid angering the Russian tsar who stood behind Austria.
answers.feedback: Nothing in the passage connects the tsar to this decision.

questions.text:
Before the canal, a ship from London to Bombay had to sail around the Cape of Good Hope, a voyage of more than ten thousand miles. Through the canal the trip was about forty percent shorter. Steamers also needed coaling stations along the way, because a ship cannot burn what it does not carry, and so ports such as Malta, Aden, and Port Said became valuable for their own sake. A great power that wanted to move quickly needed friendly harbors every few days of steaming, and that fact pulled governments into places they had never cared about before.

According to the text, why did ports such as Malta, Aden, and Port Said become valuable?

answers.text: They lay beside the Cape of Good Hope, which every ship from London to Bombay still had to round.
answers.feedback: The text says the canal let ships avoid the Cape.

answers.text: They were the only ports where quinine could be bought to protect crews from malaria and fever.
answers.feedback: The text mentions quinine in another place and does not connect it to these ports.

answers.text: They were the homes of the licensed merchants who traded with every steamer that passed through.
answers.feedback: The text gives coaling stations as the reason, not licensed merchants.

answers.text: Steamers needed coaling stations, and ships needed friendly harbors every few days of steaming.
answers.feedback: Correct. Locate, verify, and match: the text states this directly.

questions.text:

Owen pressed Parliament for a law to protect children in the mills, and an act passed in 1819, though it was weakly enforced. Owen argued that people are shaped by their surroundings and that good surroundings would make good workers. If surroundings alone make a person's character, though, there is little room left for choice and virtue. Ask yourself whether that is true.

2  By about 1816 Owen had opened a building he called the New Institution for the Formation of Character, with a school for the youngest children, who were taught through play, song, and dancing rather than the rod. The village held around two thousand people, and the mill's working day had been cut to about ten and a half hours. Grand Duke Nicholas of Russia, later Tsar Nicholas I, was among the visitors who came to see it.

3  Later Owen grew bolder. He believed a whole society could be built on shared property and cooperation, and he started a community at New Harmony, Indiana, in 1825. It broke up within a few years. His followers were among the first to be called socialists, and the word socialism began to spread.

4  The third thinker was Karl Marx, a German philosopher born in 1818. Exiled for his writings, he settled in London, where he spent his days reading in the British Museum and lived much of his life in poverty. His friend Friedrich Engels, whose family owned a cotton mill in Manchester, had written a harsh account of the workers' lives there, and Engels's income from the mill helped to support Marx. Together they published The Communist Manifesto in 1848, for a small group of exiled workers, and few people read it at the time. Its famous opening claim was that the history of all society was the history of class struggle. In the English translation of 1888 the sentence reads, "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles." In modern times, Marx said, it was a struggle between the bourgeoisie, who owned the factories and the capital, and the proletariat, who sold their labor for wages. He predicted that the workers would one day rise up, seize the factories, and end private ownership altogether, ending in a classless society. Marx spent the rest of his life on a long study of the economy, Capital, whose first volume appeared in 1867, and he died in London in 1883.

5  The heart of Capital was an argument about wages. A worker, Marx said, creates more value in a day than he is paid for, and the owner keeps the difference as profit. The more machines the owner installs, the more he can squeeze from each worker, and the wider the gap between owners and workers grows. Many economists later argued that this theory misjudged how wages and prices are set, and wages did rise over the century instead of falling. Still, the question he asked was hard to dismiss. Why did the gains of one side so often look like the losses of the other?

6  Marx wrote with real force, and he drew attention to real hardships. But judge his argument as you would any other. He claimed that economic conditions drive nearly everything else, and that ideas, religion, and law are only reflections of them. Yet the factory laws you just read about came partly from ideas, since they were driven by Christian conscience and public argument. He also predicted that workers in the most industrial country would rebel first. Britain's workers did not. Their wages rose, their unions grew, and Parliament widened the vote.
